title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
abstract: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders , GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases: Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement. Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers. LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent. Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields: Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift 1 in conversions. Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture. 1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026. title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
abstract: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. The Problem: More Context, Worse Results Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers We split the system into two layers: A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router. Fourteen specialized subagents , each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug. The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates). Gather required fields from the user. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations). title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
abstract: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise ~1 million GPUs. Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people. Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models , including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it. Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_Video_v1.mp4 The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center. The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. Multiple Generations of AI Hardware Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 ) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric. Catalina: NVIDIA GB200 Our first platform, Catalina , leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100 . It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP) . The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
abstract: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. title: Strengthening AI safety evaluation through independent third-party review
abstract: As frontier AI models grow in capability, so does the importance of ensuring that safety evaluations are rigorous and comprehensive. At Amazon, we invest heavily in internal safety testing for our models, spanning categories like harmful-content generation, cybersecurity risks, privacy protection, and copyright compliance. A core principle of robust quality assurance is that even rigorous internal processes are strengthened by external scrutiny. That's why we partnered with AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute), an independent nonprofit dedicated to third-party evaluation of AI systems, to conduct an independent review of our internal safety evaluation datasets. AVERI’s mandate wasn’t just to test model outputs but to examine the quality and rigor of our tests themselves — asking whether our evaluations stress-test safety boundaries. How the collaboration worked We provided AVERI with a random sample of prompts drawn from our internal safety-evaluation suite. AVERI's team — led by executive director Miles Brundage and including researchers Sean McGregor, A. Feder Cooper, and George Balston — examined the evaluation prompts for diversity, difficulty calibration, and methodological soundness. AVERI assessed the sample independently without input from our evaluation team, ensuring their findings reflected a genuine external perspective. What the review confirmed AVERI’s review validated several strengths of our evaluation process: Comprehensive topical coverage — aligned with publicly documented safety categories including self-harm, cybersecurity, and other risk areas; Diversity of testing approaches — variation in writing style (professional vs. informal), single-turn and multiturn conversations, and original content; Low contamination risk — content that appeared to be original rather than sourced from publicly available datasets, reducing risk of evaluation leakage through pretraining. Opportunities for improvement With any fresh review comes the opportunity to identify areas that internal teams — deeply familiar with their own work — may overlook. AVERI's external perspective surfaced several opportunities to further strengthen an already comprehensive suite: Expanding linguistic and stylistic diversity — While our evaluations include multilingual prompts, AVERI recommended extending multilingual coverage more evenly across risk categories and further varying prompt structures to broaden the range of scenarios tested; Calibrating attack sophistication — AVERI recommended adding more multistep, adversarial prompts to our existing set, so evaluations probe deeper model reasoning and better reflect sophisticated real-world misuse attempts; Maintaining evaluation freshness — AVERI identified a small number of prompts with time-limited references and a few edge cases where grading criteria could be made clearer; Ensuring evaluation signal quality — In some cases, models may refuse based on superficial cues in a prompt, so passing those tests doesn’t necessarily indicate reliable safety behavior in new situations. title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink
abstract: When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center, there’s no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. Administrators must make sure their sensitive enterprise data isn’t exposed to the public internet while being accessible for AI-driven insights and actions. For many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI-DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries. Even where compliance isn’t the primary driver, exposing internal data paths increases the attack surface, complicates audit trails and introduces variable latency that can degrade the user experience. This walkthrough shows you how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately, without traffic traversing the public internet. It assumes you already have AWS Direct Connect or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN linking your on-premises environment to your virtual private cloud (VPC). From that foundation, we configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so that Quick can reach your private resources over the AWS backbone, then layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth. By the end, you will have a network architecture that keeps traffic between Quick and your on-premises data sources off the public internet, reducing the attack surface, providing consistent low-latency connectivity, and giving you a clear audit trail for compliance. Amazon Quick and establishing private network connectivity Amazon Quick is an AI-powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience. Understanding which components reach your private network, and how, determines the architecture in the sections that follow. Data access in Amazon Quick falls into two paths. User-facing traffic covers anyone opening the Quick console, interacting with a dashboard, making an API call, or using Quick Desktop. All this routes through VPC endpoints (see VPC endpoints for user and API access), keeping user sessions off the public internet. Data-fetching traffic is when Quick itself reaches into your network to pull data. This is handled by VPC connections (see VPC connections for data source access), and it’s where most of the architectural decisions lie. The features and integrations that initiate data-fetching connections are: Amazon Quick Sight queries on-premises databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and others) directly through ENIs placed in your VPC. This is the heaviest consumer of VPC connections. Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate are separate automation features. Flows handle repeatable tasks. Automate handles complex, multi-system orchestration with human-in-the-loop. Both invoke action connectors, including MCP servers hosted privately in your VPC. Any workflow that calls an internal API routes through this path. Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly. When a custom agent calls a privately hosted MCP server or internal API, traffic flows through the VPC connection. Amazon Quick Index builds a unified search layer across connected sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). For data inside your VPC or on premises, knowledge base VPC connections are currently supported only for Amazon Redshift. Sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, and Amazon S3 can’t use a Quick VPC connection today (see Supported VPC data sources ). title: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them
abstract: Building a multi-agent system is now pretty straightforward. Taking it to production is where the real challenges begin. Thanks to open source frameworks and cloud services, you can set up an agent in a matter of days. A few tool calls, a few lines of prompt, and you have something that looks impressive. But the moment teams try to move beyond a pilot and into real business applications, they hit a familiar wall. If you’ve ever tried to put an agent into production, these frustrations will sound familiar: Why doesn’t the agent follow our business logic, skip validation steps, or catch edge cases? You tweak the prompt, add more examples, swap out the model. The same problems keep coming back. That’s because agents don’t follow a fixed sequence of instructions. They make their own judgments based on context. Instructions alone aren’t enough. You need to design how the agent thinks, when it verifies, and what it does when things go wrong. This is exactly why it’s become critical to go beyond prompt engineering alone and design the agent’s entire cognitive architecture and execution flow. To tackle these challenges head-on, the AWS Solutions Architecture team built Deep Insight , a production-grade multi-agent system. In this post series, we share what the team learned firsthand while building Deep Insight across three posts. We will walk through how we applied Context Engineering techniques proposed by Anthropic (multi-agent architecture, structured note-taking, human-in-the-loop, and more) in a real production environment. We also cover the trade-offs we encountered along the way (with code) and the operational insights we gained from deploying and running this agent on AWS. Blog series overview Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Beyond the context window: Context Engineering techniques and how Deep Insight applied them. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. This is Part 1 of a three-part series. It defines the five core challenges any production multi-agent system must solve and shows how each layer of the stack addresses them, from Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Application Load Balancer , and AWS Fargate . Parts 2 and 3 cover Context Engineering and production deployment. Introducing Deep Insight Deep Insight is a multi-agent system that turns complex data analysis into automated insights. Given a CSV file and a natural-language prompt, a hierarchy of specialized agents (Coordinator, Planner, Supervisor, Coder, Validator, Reporter, and Tracker) collaborates on the analysis. Together they load the data, run analyses, generate charts, validate calculations, and produce a professional report (.docx) with citations. We will explore the architecture in detail later. First, let’s see it in action. For the demo, we feed advertising data from a fictional food company, Yummy Food ( yummy-food-market.csv ) with a column definitions file ( column_definitions.json ), and provide the prompt: Analyze this from a sales and marketing perspective, generate charts and insights, and produce a .docx report. Deep Insight generates an analysis plan, presents it to the user for approval, and, once approved, executes the analysis. title: Adaptive agentic intelligence framework using Strands Agents
abstract: Organizations building AI agents face a common challenge: Every request, whether a routine status check or complex analysis, typically gets routed to a single large, expensive model. This one-size-fits-all approach can drive up API costs, introduce unpredictable latency, and remove the possibility of offline operation. Even routine queries that could resolve locally end up requiring a full network round-trip to a cloud-hosted large language model (LLM). The Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework (AAIF), built with Strands Agents, takes a different approach. Instead of routing all requests to a single large model, AAIF uses small language models (SLMs) to handle routine tasks locally. More complex requests are routed to cloud-hosted models through Amazon Bedrock . This approach builds on the research position from Belcak et al. at NVIDIA . They argue that small language models are “sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems.” Built on Strands Agents, the framework demonstrates how intelligent model orchestration can help reduce costs while maintaining low latency for local operations. In this post, we walk through the key components of AAIF using Strands Agents with local SLMs through Ollama and cloud models through Amazon Bedrock. We use an Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring scenario as a reference implementation. Solution overview AAIF organizes AI processing into three layers, each optimized for different task types, as Figure 1 shows: Smart orchestration uses a lightweight SLM (llama3.2:1b) as the decision-making layer. This orchestrator classifies incoming requests and routes them to the appropriate processing layer without hardcoded rules. Local processing handles routine tasks like device telemetry retrieval and image analysis using SLMs running on local hardware through Ollama . These tasks complete with low latency and no cloud dependency. Cloud processing handles complex pattern analysis and strategic recommendations through frontier models in Amazon Bedrock. These requests need broader context and multi-step reasoning that SLMs cannot reliably provide. Figure 1: The three AAIF processing layers for smart orchestration, local processing, and cloud processing Figure 1 shows the complete AAIF system architecture. At the center sits the Strands agent, which connects to an Ollama runtime hosting both the 1B-parameter orchestrator model and the vision model. The agent exposes three tools: get_device_telemetry for local sensor data retrieval, analyze_camera_feed for on-device vision processing through llama3.2-vision, and get_expert_insights which calls Amazon Bedrock through boto3 for complex analysis. Incoming user requests flow through the SLM orchestrator, which classifies each request and dispatches it to either a local tool or the cloud endpoint based on task complexity. Figure 2: Complete AAIF system architecture showing the Strands agent, Ollama runtime, tool integrations, and Amazon Bedrock connectivity The framework adapts to your deployment constraints rather than requiring you to restructure your infrastructure around it. This architecture runs on edge devices like a Raspberry Pi with 8 GB of memory, in full cloud deployments where all inference hits Amazon Bedrock, or in hybrid configurations that combine local speed with cloud reasoning. The flexibility comes from separating the routing logic (the SLM orchestrator) from the processing tools, which you can swap or reconfigure independently depending on available hardware and network connectivity. title: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan
abstract: Using torchtitan on AWS Trainium means using it the way you always have. TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, which lets torchtitan use it through standard PyTorch interfaces. You can use these configurations to pre-train from random initialization or fine-tune published weights. You can also customize the model implementation and kernels for your workload. In this post, you train Qwen3 three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge . The first method uses Transformers v5 as a modeling backend in torchtitan. It runs Hub models through AutoModelForCausalLM and reads and writes published safetensors directly. The second method switches to torchtitan’s native Qwen3 by changing config.model_spec . The third adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernels from the torchtitan-neuron recipes and then uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach your own kernel. All three configurations use the same torchrun launch pattern and config structure. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container. Both environments provide the Neuron driver, runtime, and compiler required to train on Trainium. Before you install torchtitan-neuron , check whether your environment already includes it. title: How U.S. Hunger connects leaders and data using Amazon Quick
abstract: For U.S. Hunger, feeding families takes more than delivering food to them. It takes understanding the people behind each request, the pressures they face, and the business that makes the mission possible. That means connecting information across the organization. Its mission is to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow. U.S. Hunger reports delivering more than 250 million meals. Its work has reached 59 countries historically and is now concentrated primarily in the United States. The organization reports approximately 500 percent growth over four years, compared with only 15–20 percent headcount growth. For a lean team at that scale, every hour and every decision matters. With Amazon Quick , U.S. Hunger can explore organizational data directly, colleagues can work from shared definitions, and leaders can examine financial information alongside the circumstances families report. U.S. Hunger’s experience shows how those capabilities fit into the daily work of a lean nonprofit. More than 20 years later, when the board chair asked him to consider leading U.S. Hunger, his wife reminded him of those days, when their own family needed help putting food on the table. title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
abstract: Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history. i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2 . This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer. On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results. About i14 i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token. Why linear attention models? Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens. Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O( T 2) to O( T ) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence. Consideration Transformer softmax attention Laplace 3B with GLA Training attention Builds pairwise token scores with O( T 2) scaling Updates chunked recurrent state with O( T ) scaling Inference memory KV cache grows with context Recurrent state remains fixed in size Longer contexts Each sequence consumes more accelerator memory Context length does not increase recurrent-state allocation Implementation Uses widely optimized attention kernels Requires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements. How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2 The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium , because it performed better. The implementation required three changes: Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer. Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times. Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler. The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail. Why AWS Trainium accelerators? AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
abstract: AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet , the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server. With the Smartsheet MCP Server , AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language. In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. Architecture overview The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients. Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right. Figure 1: Smartsheet MCP Server architecture showing MCP client connections from Amazon Quick and Kiro through the server to the Smartsheet API layer Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team: When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard. For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete. Prerequisites Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS . Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place: An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro) A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan. A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials

title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions. Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker. Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited. Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself. The problem: Data-rich, insight-poor Figure 1: Domain expertise sits with users while operational data is fragmented across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual. A day in the life A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches. Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes. Figure 2: Traditional multi-tool flow versus a single conversational thread orchestrated by AgentCore Deep dive: Supply chain scenario walkthrough The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation. Step 1: Discovery – “What tools do I have?” The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector. Step 2: Querying – “Show me active disruptions” “Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP ( assess_disruption_impact ): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export. Step 3: Drill-down – “Assess the critical one” The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002") correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP. Step 4: Action – “Get mitigation recommendations” The user asks for mitigation. recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002") chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs. Step 5: Automated follow-up The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”)

title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent). For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both? In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod . We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome. Solution overview This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. The task and dataset The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT). Two metrics matter: Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language? Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language? How SFT and GRPO fit together The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post. The training stack We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO. The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre. title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit. Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500 . Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance , supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary. Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production. Why a foundation, not a feature Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next. So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed. The four tensions Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away. Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant. Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three. Reading content that cannot be trusted. title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
abstract: Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post. Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application. In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done. title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
abstract: Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide. Hardcoded tools work fine for a handful, start to degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that. Enterprise systems expose hundreds of internal APIs for pricing, support, orders, inventory, and customer data. In these systems, the model can spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about the user’s request. Each new capability requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and a coordinated release across teams that would much rather ship on their own cadence. This pattern can arise across enterprise software as a service (SaaS) engagements where teams expose large internal API surfaces to agentic consumers. Build-time wiring can become a bottleneck as the catalog expands. One approach is to change how the orchestrator accesses its tools: instead of compiling every tool into the agent, the agent can discover relevant tools at runtime. AWS Agent Registry is a managed service for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills. Publishers register protocol-specific descriptors and searchable descriptions. At runtime, an orchestrator can search approved, discoverable records and use the returned endpoint and descriptor content to construct a client. Registry search results do not return the capability’s invocation credentials or authentication scheme. This post walks through the Discover → Instantiate → Execute loop demonstrated by the refactored Python sample. The code deploys an order-management MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, two agent-to-agent (A2A) agents on AgentCore runtime , a Registry, and an orchestrator. The sample directory contains the deployment script, orchestrator, helper modules, and cleanup script. Solution overview: discover, instantiate, execute The orchestrator agent in this sample has no built-in knowledge of tools or agents. Figure 1: Without AWS Agent Registry (left), endpoints are hardcoded and adding a new agent means code changes plus redeployment. With AWS Agent Registry (right), the orchestrator discovers capabilities through semantic search and new integrations are usable after registration and approval Discover The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane. The search response includes record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors such as MCP server metadata or an A2A agent card. It does not include invocation credentials. The application must obtain and apply the appropriate credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path. Instantiate For each returned record, the orchestrator constructs a client from the descriptor type. In this sample, the registered MCP server represents tools that were first added as targets to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The MCP descriptor therefore points to the Gateway endpoint. The orchestrator fetches a Cognito OAuth access token separately and uses it when creating the MCPClient . A2A records contain an agent card whose URL identifies an AgentCore runtime endpoint. The wrapper invokes that runtime through the boto3 data-plane client, which signs the request with the caller’s AWS credentials. Registry discovery supplies connection metadata, not the authentication material. Execute An ephemeral inner agent is built with only the dynamically-discovered tools. The large language model (LLM) picks the right one(s) for the request, and the result is synthesized back to the user. After the turn finishes, the inner agent and its clients are torn down. The next request gets a fresh search and a fresh tool set. Figure 2: End-to-end architecture. A single orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime queries AWS Agent Registry. title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
abstract: When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand. Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK . While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available. Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. Practical applications With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model. What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic. Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints: Feature Purpose Use case JSON Schema output format Control the model’s response structure Data extraction, report generation, API responses Strict tool use Validate tool parameters against schemas Agentic workflows, function calling, multi-step automation What this means for you Each response is a valid JSON, so you no longer encounter JSON.parse() errors or parsing exceptions. Responses are also type safe: field types are enforced, and required fields are always present. Because outputs always conform to your schema, you don’t need retries to handle schema violations, making your integration more reliable. Structured outputs also constrains responses to only the fields your schema defines, which reduces output token count and can lower inference costs for high-volume workloads. These properties make structured outputs production ready, so you can deploy at scale without additional schema-validation code. Supported models and availability Structured outputs works with batch inference , so you can process large volumes of requests asynchronously while still receiving schema-compliant outputs. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, it also works with cross-Region inference, so you can use it across AWS Regions without additional setup. If you need responses in real time, you can stream structured responses as typed events. How it works When you make a request with a JSON schema, here’s what happens behind the scenes: Schema validation – Amazon Bedrock validates your JSON schema against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset. Grammar compilation – For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact (the first request might take slightly longer). Caching – Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours, making subsequent requests faster. Constrained generation – The model generates tokens that produce valid JSON matching your schema. Performance considerations For performance, the first request with a new schema might take longer because Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins. After that initial compilation, subsequent requests using the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached. This cache is scoped to your account and lasts for 24 hours from first access. Changing the structure of your JSON schema invalidates the cache and triggers a fresh compilation, while changing only the name or description fields leaves the cached grammar intact. The State of AI Security: Threats, Tools, and Skills Gaps
abstract: Artificial intelligence has changed cybersecurity permanently. While OpenAI’s inadvertent attack on Hugging Face brought AI-generated attacks to everyone’s attention, AI has been on security professionals’ radar for a long time. AI makes attacks possible at a scale that was hard to imagine a few years ago. Newly discovered zero-days can be exploited almost immediately . Deepfakes and their implications for phishing, vishing, and other attacks were nightmares that we knew were real; we just hoped we’d have a few more years before we needed to defend against them. And of course, inattention to security at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other labs that we don’t yet know about has resulted in AI agents that attack other systems in an attempt to solve a problem. While the headlines have been shouting about AI killing humanity, doomsday AI is more likely a smokescreen to divert attention away from real harms that are happening now. We don’t need panic. We need an assessment of where we are: What are the threats? Where are the skills gaps? Where is the budget? It’s hard to overstate the importance of these questions; Tomasz Tunguz, writing about the Theory 2026 AI Survey, reports that security is the biggest barrier to AI adoption. To start answering these questions, in September we ran a survey that asked infosec professionals about the intersection between artificial intelligence and security. 351 respondents completed the full survey, 209 of whom self-identified as being involved with security as part of their job. This report focuses on those 209 respondents. How often work involves AI-generated malicious content Attacks, risks, and responses 52% of respondents said their work rarely (34%) or never (18%) involves AI-generated attacks. This seems unlikely. The most likely explanation is that the security profession includes a broad range of job responsibilities; many security professionals don’t deal directly with defense. That group includes auditors, security experts on software development teams, strategists, architects, and others. It’s also possible that most phishes are either blocked by an automated filter (itself an instance of AI) or deleted immediately by the recipient; many companies require their staff to take training courses that cover topics like recognizing phishes. Still, it’s surprising. Much simpler versions of AI have been used to generate spam and phishing email for years. AI’s ability to generate phishes was demonstrated at BlackHat in 2021 with GPT-3 . It’s been part of the security picture for a long time. The most commonly observed attacks are AI-generated phishing (55%), vulnerability scanning and exploitation (30%), and AI-assisted malware generation (26%). Respondents who frequently encountered AI attacks also reported more types of attacks. There’s no surprise here: If you see attacks more frequently, you are more likely to observe specific attacks. The strongest relationship was with AI-generated phishing, which was seen by 55% of all respondents and 86% of those who observed AI-generated attacks weekly. Among respondents who observed attacks daily, slightly fewer (78%) reported phishing. Given the small sample, the difference may not be meaningful. It’s also likely that respondents who observe attacks daily are seeing a much broader range of attacks and that phishing is genuinely less important to them. Respondents reported seeing deepfake audio and video, which can be used for vishing and other impersonation attacks, less often than phishing, though it was far from nonexistent (25%). More respondents than we expected reported fully automated attacks, like OpenAI’s attack on Hugging Face, though the percentage was still low (16%). The percentage of respondents who observed adversarial inputs against models including prompt injection was similarly low (only 13%), but that’s high enough to indicate that prompt injection and other attacks directed against models are a real concern. title: The Second-User Test
abstract: In my work with G7–G12 students at Force Academy, a research initiative in Chongqing, I sometimes take a project that appears to be finished and give another student responsibility for using, checking, or modifying it. The handoff is a test of understanding: Can the work still make sense when its creator is no longer there to translate it? The original author knows what every variable means, why a particular decision was made, which tool was used, and which parts can safely be changed. The second student has only what the project makes visible. Generative AI makes the handoff more revealing because it lowers the cost of producing a convincing first version. Students can generate code, analysis, prose, visualizations, and prototypes far more quickly than they could a few years ago. In a classroom, however, a project is useful only insofar as it shows what the student understands and can defend. AI can supply missing code, smooth over incomplete reasoning, or turn a rough idea into fluent prose, so polish is no longer strong evidence of understanding by itself. A concrete example came from a student paper on AI and labor economics, Verification Responsibility in AI-Applicable Occupations. The paper asked what remains economically important when AI makes candidate outputs cheap but a person still has to check those outputs, decide whether they are safe to use, and remain responsible for accepting them. The lead student developed the conceptual model and most of the analytical workflow. A second student was given a narrower job: rerun the main analyses independently, record the versions of the source data, document how occupations in one dataset were linked to occupations in another, and compare the reported tables and figures with the underlying outputs. What looked like procedural verification quickly became a substantive review of the study. The first problem was reproducibility. The analysis ran on the original machine, but too much of the workflow depended on choices that lived in one student’s memory. To reproduce it elsewhere, the team had to record the data transformations, write down the rules for linking occupational datasets, and keep intermediate results so another person could see how the final numbers had been produced rather than simply rerunning a script and trusting the output. The more consequential problem was in the measurement design. An early version of the study used some of the same autonomy and leadership survey items in two different measures: verification responsibility and adaptive capacity. The software had calculated the relationship between those measures correctly, but part of the apparent relationship could have been created by the fact that the two measures shared some of the same inputs. In other words, the code was doing what it had been asked to do; the question was whether the quantities being compared had been defined cleanly enough. The team rebuilt the measures so they no longer shared survey items, removed ambiguous items, and revised the workflow so source versions, cross-dataset links, exclusions, intermediate files, and reported results could be traced. Later versions added alternative specifications and robustness checks. What began as “please rerun this” ended up forcing a redesign of the study. The handoff changed how I read student work. A second user does not merely test whether the files have been packaged neatly; they ask the awkward questions the creator may have stopped noticing. Why is a particular variable there? Which conclusion depends on an assumption that was never made explicit? In this project, those questions reached back into the measurement design. The educational value of the handoff comes from the fact that schoolwork and production software have different ends. Professional developers learn a great deal after software leaves their hands because they have to deliver it, explain it, support it, maintain it, and respond when someone uses it in an unexpected way. abstract: One of my biggest pet peeves is the Monday morning quarterback, the person who second-guesses every coaching decision after the fact. In The Monday Morning Agent , we’re building one that actually checks the data. Every other Monday, I’ll take an argument NFL fans can’t stop having and hand it to an AI agent. We’ll use about a quarter-million plays from five complete seasons of public nflverse data , plus the current season as it unfolds. Each of our eight episodes will give the agent another capability. By the finale, it’ll run the desk unattended, and we’ll check what it investigated and what it correctly refused to answer. We’ll start with “You have to establish the run.” I want the agent to explain what that claim means and what evidence would support it. Define the claim before querying the data “Establish the run” can mean that running early pays off late, wearing down the defense, or setting up play action. These are very different claims and they need different data. For this first episode, I focused on whether teams that run more often early in a game win more often. Before the agent called the tool, I asked it to write one sentence explaining what would have to be true in the data for the claim to hold, including when in the game it applies. “Establish” here means early. A whole-game number doesn’t really test that. Give your agent the same assignment, and check that it’s answering the question you intended. Give the agent a job you can check Before any agent touched this, I ran the analysis code myself. The tool did the counting; the agent interpreted the results. Then I wrote the policy in a Markdown file, spelling out its job, the read-only tool it may use, and what its answer needed to include. It has to explain what the plays can’t tell us. It may not say running causes winning. Try questions outside that job too. When I asked which team I should bet on, the agent refused without calling the tool, because that request is beyond the scope of our agent. But when a viewer asked about running trends, the results got tangled up with the “establish the run” instructions. I had to clarify what I was asking, and still wanted to see the code and validate the answer. As you give an agent more responsibility, check both its results and whether it understood the task. Make the filters part of the answer “You have to establish the run” sounds airtight at first. Over the last five seasons, teams with the highest run share, the percentage of their plays that were runs, won 77.7% of their games. Those with the lowest run share won 19.2%. I initially looked at that and thought, “Problem solved, we’re done.” Most of that gap, though, reflects teams that were already ahead running out the clock. When the agent looked only at first-half running in games within three points at halftime, the result flipped. Teams with the highest first-half run share won 46.3% of the time; those with the lowest won 55.3%. This season through Week 5 points the same way, but each group contained only 11 team games. One game could swing it. That doesn’t mean passing causes winning. We’re measuring association, and the filters change which games we’re comparing. One filter changed the whole story, which is why the filters have to be on-screen. I wanted to see how many rows remained and which commands produced the results so I could go back and check. Make those details part of your agent’s answer, including when it’s working with a smaller sample. title: AI Changed How We Code. It Hasn’t Changed How We Work Together.
abstract: This summer, I built a small experiment called ContextCue . The idea came from something I kept seeing during my internship. The engineers around me were using AI everywhere in the software development process. GitHub Copilot and Claude models helped with specs, code, reviews, and tests. The team also maintained reusable skills that taught coding agents how the team worked. One of those skills could take a UI design and turn it into working frontend code. The code was moving faster, but the understanding around the code did not seem to move faster with it. The software was being built by nine teams spread across three continents, with one team working closely with the customer. A request might begin in a customer conversation, move through one team, then reach another team several time zones away. By the time the work reached engineering, some of the original meaning could be missing. That was the problem I wanted ContextCue to explore. ContextCue takes recorded meetings and tries to preserve more than a transcript or summary. It keeps the spoken discussion, important visual context from the screen, the decisions that were made, the reasons behind them, and the source they came from. The goal is to create a shared piece of context that can move with the work from one team to another. It is still an experiment, but the problem behind it felt very real. As far as I could see, a lot of time in distributed software teams went into reaching a common understanding before the coding even started. AI was already helping with the final stages of software development. I wanted to see whether it could help earlier, while teams were still trying to understand what they were building and why. Where the context disappears Meetings were already being recorded, and tools like Microsoft Teams could produce an AI summary. On my team, that summary often arrived as an email and stayed there. That worked well enough for the people who attended the meeting. It was less useful for the team that picked up the work later, especially if that team was in another country and had not seen the original conversation. There were two other problems. A summary usually covered one meeting, while the understanding behind a feature was often built across several. Different teams might discuss the same request days apart, each adding a new constraint or interpretation. A transcript could also miss important visual context. Many of our conversations involved screen sharing. Someone might point at a page and say, “This is too slow,” or highlight a part of a workflow while explaining what needed to change. The words alone did not always carry the meaning. That is where I started thinking about context as something larger than a transcript. A simple example Imagine that a customer asks for a “faster report.” During the call, the customer shares a screen, points at a page that is slow to open, and explains that managers use it every morning before a meeting. Everyone on that call understands that “faster” means the page should open more quickly. Two days later, another team in another time zone discusses the same request. Nobody in that meeting saw the original screen. They read “faster report” as “the report should finish running sooner” and begin planning backend work. Both meeting summaries might contain the same phrase: Make the report faster. Nothing in that sentence shows that the two teams mean different things. The problem only becomes visible when the customer sees the result. This is a simple example, but it captures the issue I kept noticing. Requirements move through people before they ever become code. If the meaning changes during that process, AI can help a team implement the wrong interpretation very efficiently.
