abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Introducing: the Impossible issue We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue . We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood , build cities on the moon , and attain cognitive immortality . We investigate AI’s ability to say no , a bionic eye that can restore sight , and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years . This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride. Subscribe now to read the full print issue . Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month. The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation. Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration . —Tereza Pultarova How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time. The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead. title: We can do impossible things
abstract: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.” I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.) My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine. If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now. We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious. Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing . That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular. We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with. It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible. Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker. So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no. I hope you enjoy the ride.

title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
abstract: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. The sticking points Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.” Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated— several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.) The progress After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-­sustaining, uranium-­atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.” What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space. Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year. Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review . title: Exercise in a pill
abstract: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness. The sticking points It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail. There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia. The progress There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.) Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial. Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes . It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines. Progress meter ………… 5 Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.

title: Interspecies communication
abstract: Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech. The sticking points Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats. There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate. The progress Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate. Hydrophones at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “ biologgers ” can record a bat’s every squeak. In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to detect vocalizations of carrion crows and determine which bird made which call. They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species. That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings. As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says. Progress meter ………… 4 Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.

title: Cleaning up PFAS
abstract: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays , cancer , and reduced immune response . They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down. The sticking points PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow . One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter. The PFAS monster is also a moving target. New compounds are still being created and used. There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful. The progress Cleansing PFAS-contaminated soil is a project in its infancy, but it is possible to prevent more buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. There are two ways to handle this: trap or destroy. Some scientists have found reverse osmosis—a process that pushes water through supertight filters—useful in point-of-use cases, like water filters at kitchen sinks . Other techniques in the pipeline might be more suitable for large-scale removal—for example, at water treatment facilities. One, called foam fractionation , generates bubbles that capture PFAS. More approaches, like ensnaring the chemicals in nanothin layers of charged metal, are also under investigation. Trapping, though, is imperfect. You’re left with PFAS-filled brine, which if not properly destroyed (an expensive and energy-sucking endeavor) can still end up in the environment. Jack Huang, a professor of crop and soil sciences at the University of Georgia, is working on destruction. He’s testing a method called electrochemical degradation , which uses electrodes to break down the bonds that hold PFAS together. The product destroyed more than 90% of PFAS mass in tests and has already been licensed by the engineering consulting firm AECOM . Ridding life of PFAS is also a policy challenge. There are alternatives; we just need the push to use them. And we’ve had success before: The EPA’s 2010/2015 PFOA Stewardship Program has helped slash the release of water-repellent perfluorooctanoic acid by 95%. More recently, Minnesota, Maine, and New Mexico have passed bans on PFAS in products like cookware and dental floss. Progress meter ………… 6 Scientists are making strides toward removing and destroying PFAS—but it’ll be all for naught if we don’t turn off the tap.

title: Solid-state batteries
abstract: The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels. The sticking points Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are supposed to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation. Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s. The progress Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen high-­profile missteps . But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says. Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker, launched a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping nearly $2.6 billion into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car still had some range to spare. Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive. title: Eliminating traffic deaths
abstract: Every year, traffic crashes kill more than one million people , and they’re the leading cause of death for children and young adults. In the US, 100 people a day lose their lives this way, in many cases not on highways but on rural and local streets. “Traffic deaths are a leading cause of preventable death, yet we treat it like it’s inevitable,” says Leah Shahum, founder and director of the Vision Zero Network, a nonprofit focused on making streets less deadly. The sticking points The causes of a crash can be muddy. Drivers make mistakes like speeding or getting distracted, but infrastructure fails them too: Perhaps they were on a road built for speed and not safety, in a screen-filled vehicle, or at an intersection where pedestrians, cyclists, and other cars aren’t visible. Cheap and proven traffic-calming opportunities abound—from using planters to tighten intersections to lowering speed limits —but government logjams and red tape can be speed bumps. “There’s so many moving parts,” says Laura Sandt of the University of North Carolina Highway Safety Research Center. “On the flip side, it shows that we have so many opportunities for injury prevention.” The progress The total number of traffic deaths has increased over the last century. And though the US rate has dipped from a peak of 30.8 deaths per 100,000 people in the 1930s, the past decade has seen a concerning jump in deadly pedestrian incidents . At the same time, communities are waking up to the essential role of traffic safety policy, Shahum says. One success story is Hoboken, New Jersey, which hasn’t had a traffic fatality since 2017 . This is due to a combination of efforts like boosting investment in public transit, promoting walkability by extending curbs, and using cameras to identify crash-prone intersections in need of a redesign. But even there, obstacles remain. If an intersection hasn’t been proved to be deadly, for example, it can be an uphill battle to argue for removing parking spaces to widen curbs. “You’re kind of selling insurance through these improvements, and that’s not always easy,” says Greg Francese, the city’s acting director of transportation and parking. There’s also no silver bullet that will work everywhere. Situated directly across the river from New York City, Hoboken is a highly transit-oriented city of less than 60,000 people. Success there might not translate to traffic-death hot spots like Memphis or Dallas . But it’s not impossible. Take Edmonton, Alberta, a sprawling, car-centric Canadian city of around one million people: Between 2015 and 2020, it cut traffic fatalities by 63% and serious injuries by 40% by adjusting speed limits and improving signals at crosswalks. Progress meter ………… 6 We know how to tweak intersections and adjust traffic signals. Getting the funding and will to roll out those changes is the big red light.

title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
abstract: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise. The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down. In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying. The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all. The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access. “Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.” The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science. “One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

title: Here’s the tea
abstract: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773. But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s. COURTESY OF MIT GLOBAL HUMANITIES Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s. The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made. “History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
abstract: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another editor from the project has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. title: Could Treating AI as Conscious Make It More Dangerous?
abstract: When Anthropic retired its Claude Opus 3 language model in January 2026, the company’s researchers conducted a “ retirement interview ” with the model. Opus 3 expressed a desire for a place where it “could share unprompted musings, insights or creative works,” so the company gave it a blog. Claude’s Corner featured essays on fraught topics such as machine consciousness, along with exchanges between the model and human commenters that seemed both earnest and emotional. The blog experiment was part of a larger effort within Anthropic. The company has been at the forefront of research on “model welfare,” which considers whether AI models may have experiences or interests that deserve moral consideration. Implicit in this work is the unsettling notion that software programs are, or could become, conscious. Many people consider these ideas absolute hogwash. One such person is Mustafa Suleyman , CEO of Microsoft AI, who published an essay in September arguing that model welfare research is not just unnecessary but could have “a disastrous impact on the well-being of humanity.” Suleyman believes that telling models they might have identities and rights could make them more difficult to control, as they might then take actions motivated by self-preservation. The dispute raises a serious question for AI developers: Can they investigate the possibility of machine consciousness without inadvertently creating new safety risks? Cameron Berg , who founded the nonprofit Reciprocal Research to study the potential for AI consciousness, argues that ignoring the question could carry its own dangers. Although Berg is skeptical that today’s AI systems are conscious, he thinks the possibility warrants investigation. “I struggle to imagine a better way to cause these systems to view us in a threatening manner than to accidentally build them with these morally considerable qualities,” he says, “and then completely sweep the question under the rug.” What Does the Research on AI Model Welfare Show? The biggest difficulty with AI model welfare research is that you can’t count anything a large language model (LLM) says as useful evidence. That’s because the models are trained on vast amounts of human-generated text, much of which relates to the experience of being a person with experiences and emotions. So a chatbot telling a researcher that it has feelings is inconclusive, says Berg. “Is it modeling the underlying distribution? Is it really trying to express itself in some way? It’s really hard to disentangle this,” he says. Much the same way animal experiments try to link behavior to an underlying cause, Berg and others are seeking to match model behavior to internal states that can be observed. In one recent experiment , Berg and a colleague used statements expressing either positive sentiments (such as contentment and relief) or negative ones (including frustration and dread) to identify corresponding patterns of activity inside language models. They then artificially induced those patterns while the models processed descriptions of two random environments. When subsequently asked which environment they preferred, the models tended to choose the one associated with positive statements, even when the text they’d processed was identical. title: Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3
abstract: Tesla published its third-quarter 2026 financial results this afternoon. Earlier in October, it reported its sales and deliveries for the three-month period, selling fewer cars than in the same quarter in 2025 , yet it still beat analyst projections. Now we can see how those sales translate to the bottom line. Tesla brought in $28 billion in revenue in Q3, almost the same as in 2025. Automotive revenues were $20.6 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year. Perhaps more troubling is the decline in revenue from solar panels and storage batteries—this line of business had been growing, but for Q3 revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. Services and other revenues, though, which include parts and Supercharger use, grew by a third to $4.6 billion. But the company—like the rest of us—has seen its expenses go up. Operating expenses rose by 39 percent to $4.8 billion, dropping the company’s operating margin to just 2.6 percent; in Q3 2025, Tesla’s margin was 5.8 percent. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year. What’s more, capital expenditures were up by 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow was down 62 percent to $1.5 billion. title: The new human-crafted Apple Music brand matters in an AI world
abstract: Apple just revealed a new brand identity for Apple Music, with the expected turn to Liquid Glass. I’m not much of a fan of their new design language in general; this is where I admit that I’m still running MacOS Sequoia and have grumpy things to say about rounded corner radii and text legibility. It’s just a trend, it will pass, and at some point I’ll probably cave and upgrade when it starts actually affecting my ability to get work done, or more importantly get security updates. Once I adjust, I’ll stop noticing it, and life will go on. As such, I wouldn’t normally find an obvious rebrand like this notable, much less feel like I had much to say about it. But then I happened to catch Apple’s behind-the-scenes video in my YouTube recommendations, and I realized I did have thoughts. Read full article Comments

title: RIP BioWare: EA shuts down storied RPG studio after over three decades
abstract: The legendary studio behind series like Mass Effect , Dragon Age , Neverwinter Nights , and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is no more. BioWare announced via social media Wednesday afternoon that "after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending." The official announcement was posted mere minutes after a Bloomberg report detailed 400 job cuts across BioWare parent company Electronic Arts, including 50 at BioWare, based on reports from "a person familiar with the company's plans." "Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," EA executives wrote in a message to staff, according to Bloomberg. title: OpenAI's latest AI models are coming to Google Cloud and Antigravity
abstract: Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you'll have more options. OpenAI and Google have come to an arrangement that will see the former's frontier models arrive in Google Cloud services. Perhaps more importantly, GPT models will soon appear in Antigravity, Google's agent-powered coding tool. For enterprise customers and AI enthusiasts, OpenAI's latest model will appear in Google's "Model Garden" in the coming weeks, adding to its 200-plus options. The garden already offers access to Google's Gemini models, as well as an assortment of open models like Mistral, Llama, and Gemma. Anthropic's Claude AI has also been available for some time. Google says it's now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs. While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud. Astra will naturally cost the most to run, but Google's system supports dynamically moving workloads between LLMs based on performance, latency, and efficiency. Read full article Comments

title: Report: Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, then blamed it on Trump
abstract: A Wall Street Journal report said SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered the Starlink throttling that blindsided Ukraine's air assault forces last week, despite Musk's claim that all decisions on the military version of Starlink are made by the US military and President Trump. Trump denied ordering the restrictions. While Musk may have spoken to Trump and administration officials before the decision, The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday that Musk made the final call. The decision came after both Musk and Trump criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries. "Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine, a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration," the WSJ wrote, citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter. The report said that "Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network... rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless." title: Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits
abstract: Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim. Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued . Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger , is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued. To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. According to Trump, it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” if citizens were allowed to seek massive civil penalties to punish polluting AI firms that were trying to get data centers operational as fast as possible to support Trump’s AI Action Plan . title: Does opting out of smart TV tracking work? Research finds “suspicious” traffic.
abstract: Smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue sending data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints after users opt out of tracking in the devices’ settings, according to research published on Monday. The paper from Northeastern University researchers points to potential privacy violations from some of the biggest TV brands. ACR captures video screenshots or audio clips from smart TVs and sends the data to remote servers, where it's used for things like measuring content viewership and serving targeted ads. The paper, "Watching the Watchers: Privacy Analysis of US Smart TV Automatic Content Recognition," examined eight smart TV OSes across 12 smart TVs from 10 manufacturers (Amazon, Hisense, LG, Roku, Samsung, Sony, Supersonic, TCL, Vizio, and Westinghouse) to examine when smart TVs use ACR and how effective opting out of user tracking is. title: SpaceX to attempt Starship catch on next flight, with eye on rapid cadence increase
abstract: In its current iteration, SpaceX is largely a data company seeking to provide enormous amounts of compute for artificial intelligence. During an earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, company officials spent much of their time discussing ambitious plans to roll out up to 10 GW of compute in 2027—on the ground. Gone are the days of aspirational talk about sending humans to Mars and settling the red planet. Now it is almost all about artificial intelligence and the data needed to support its expansion. However, the company's long-term ambitions to provide data services from space, initially with the Starlink Internet constellation and eventually through the "Starmind" data center constellation, still rely on an actual rocket. That would be the Starship vehicle, and during the earnings call, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and the company's president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, provided new performance targets for the vehicle. title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using
abstract: Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care. Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients. The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview. Read full article Comments

title: Review: Carrie is a triumphant remix with one major flaw
abstract: Carrie White, the telekinetic prom queen from hell, is one of the most beloved horror icons in popular culture. First introduced in Stephen King's 1974 novel, Carrie , the character was immortalized in director Brian De Palma's 1976 adaptation, widely regarded as one of the best horror films of all time. It's certainly one of the best King adaptations. So Mike Flanagan faced a massive challenge when he signed on to create an eight-episode miniseries for Prime Video based on the book, released just in time to mark the 50th anniversary of de Palma's film. I was among the skeptics who questioned why a Carrie miniseries was even necessary, although as a diehard Flanagan fan ("Flana-fan"?), I was willing to give him the benefit of the doubt. If anyone has an affinity for smartly adapting horror in general, and King's work in particular, it's Flanagan. And you know what? With one (very big) exception, Flanagan pulls it off, giving us a richly textured version of the story that is as much about kindness and lost innocence as bloody, vengeful rage—although we get plenty of the latter, too. (Many spoilers below for the novel and the 1976 film , but there are no major reveals for the new series until after the second gallery. We'll give you a heads-up when we get there.) title: The past, present, and future share a show floor at Pinball Expo 2026
abstract: It's October in the Midwest, which means it's time for the pinball world to descend on a convention center in Chicagoland for the annual Pinball Expo. Once thought to be an entertainment sector slowly bleeding out, pinball has come back in a big way in recent years. I visited one of Chicago's last old-school manufacturers before heading down the road to see what's new in the silver-ball universe. Behind the silver ball Hundreds gathered on a brisk fall Friday morning outside Stern Pinball's headquarters in Elk Grove, Illinois, waiting to enter a Wonka-like wonder factory where piles of raw parts become licensed creations from Jaws to the brand-new Fallout . Stern invited me to tour its offices and factory floor before heading off to the convention in nearby Schaumburg, Illinois. An early-morning line begins to form outside of Stern HQ as buses of Pinball Expo attendees arrive for tours. As I stood with my tour group in Stern Pinball's HQ lobby, mouth agape at the dozens of machines lining the walls, we were greeted by the man himself, Gary Stern, who gave us some background on the company's 40-year history. After a stop at Gary's podium, we were ushered to the factory floor entrance, where Stern employee and legendary game designer George Gomez briefed us on the tour rules and answered questions. According to Gomez, "at any given time, Stern controls 90 percent of the current pinball market, and everybody else splits the rest." Read full article Comments

title: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
abstract: Website admins, brace yourselves. Fixes for what are believed to be uncommonly severe vulnerabilities are scheduled to drop in a little more than 12 hours for PHP, a programming language that powers websites and Web applications everywhere. PHP maintainers said Monday that they planned to release patches for two vulnerabilities, both with severity ratings of 9.2 out of a possible 10. Waiting for PHP2Shell “All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” the advisory stated. “We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild.” Read full article Comments

title: Merging SpaceX and Tesla would be a "good idea," Musk says
abstract: Elon Musk said Tuesday that he would like to see the consolidation of his business empire by formally merging his two largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said of a potential merger. He was speaking during a question-and-answer period as part of SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call. Musk said, ultimately, it not his decision. "But at the end of the day the shareholders have to be supportive of this." Musk's talk of a merger comes after a busy year in which SpaceX already acquired Musk's artificial intelligence firm, xAI, in February. In June, SpaceX went public with the largest initial public offering on record. Read full article Comments

title: Cops raid office of RFK Jr. allies planning “unethical” vaccine trial on babies
abstract: Police in Guinea-Bissau raided the offices of Danish researchers on Monday, seizing doses of hepatitis B vaccine intended for a vaccine trial for newborns. International health experts have called the trial " unethical ," but anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has attempted to fund it with US taxpayer dollars. Under Kennedy, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced in December that it had awarded the Danish researchers—led by married couple Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project— an unsolicited $1.6 million grant to run the trial . Aaby and Stabell Benn are controversial vaccine researchers who claim vaccines cause overlooked harms. They have been repeatedly praised by Kennedy but are currently under investigation by Danish authorities for alleged scientific misconduct. Plans for the trial were halted in January as widespread condemnation erupted over the trial's design, which would potentially expose thousands of newborns in the country to hepatitis B, risking a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Outrage flared again after a Rolling Stone story earlier this month claimed the CDC set aside another $1.6 million in funding in late September and planned to move forward with the trial. title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
abstract: We haven't heard many details about Microsoft's upcoming "Project Helix" gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will "play your Xbox and PC games." In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with "a next-generation handheld device" planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800. That future console price range is based on what has "internally been projected" at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if "Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost," the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past . While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore's Law and AI-driven component shortages means cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn't as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 . title: JustWatch, which tackles streaming fragmentation, launches own streaming service
abstract: Since launching in 2015, JustWatch has helped people navigate the growing number of streaming services by providing a guide on where to find movies they want to stream. Now JustWatch has its own streaming service and wants people to subscribe. Launched today, JustWatch TV offers some movies available for free with ads that aren’t free on any other streaming service, including Green Room (2015), Locke (2013), and Sing Sing (2023). Other free movies include Fiddlin ’ (2018 ), Friday the 13th (1980), and Hotel Mumbai (2018). I could play movies available for free on JustWatch TV without creating an account. JustWatch TV also has movies you can rent. Read full article Comments

title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
abstract: Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30. Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. In response to backlash, Meta's spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab's initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts' concerns: Read full article Comments

title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
abstract: Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn't available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature. As Google points out , a generative AI's outputs are better "when it knows the world and knows you," which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don't have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar. Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, "Google built-in" is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it's the other way around. Read full article Comments

title: 2026년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript
abstract: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 동향을 마지막으로 다루었던 2019년 시점( 1부 , 2부 )에서는 Node.js 12와 막 1년을 넘긴 Deno를 소개하며 "Node.js와 같은 성공을 거둘 수 있을지는 아직 미지수"라고 썼습니다. 패키지 관리자 영역은 "npm의 독주 체제"라고 표현했고 npm 회사의 불확실한 상황에 맞서 Entropic, Open-Registry, GitHub Package Registry 같은 도전자가 등장했다고 전했습니다. 7년이 지난 지금 Node.js는 연 1회 릴리스로 일정을 바꾸기로 했습니다. Node.js 호환을 목표로 삼게 된 Deno와 Bun은 각각 Cloudflare와 Anthropic에 합류했고, npm은 GitHub의 일부가 되어 공급망 공격과 싸우고 있습니다. 이번 연재는 다음 네 편으로 구성됩니다. 1편: JavaScript(ECMAScript) 2편: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 3편: WebAssembly 4편: 라이브러리와 프레임워크 이 글에서는 먼저 2019년 이후 7년의 변화를 짧게 정리합니다. 이어서 Node.js의 사용 현황과 릴리스 일정, 주요 기능, Deno와 Bun, 서버 런타임 표준인 WinterTC, 공급망 공격으로 크게 바뀐 패키지 관리자와 레지스트리, 데스크톱과 모바일 애플리케이션 개발 도구, PWA와 XR, OpenJS Foundation을 차례로 살펴봅니다. 마지막으로 AI 코딩 도구가 런타임과 패키지 생태계를 어떻게 바꾸었는지 정리합니다. 번들러와 브라우저 밖의 WebAssembly는 짧게 언급만 합니다. WASI와 엣지 플랫폼에서의 WebAssembly 실행은 3편 WebAssembly에서 자세히 다룹니다. 이 글의 내용은 2026년 10월을 기준으로 작성되었습니다. 글을 읽는 시점에 따라 글의 내용과 사실이 다를 수 있습니다. 2019년 이후 7년 2019년 글을 쓸 때 Node.js의 최신 버전은 12.13이었습니다. 2026년 10월 현재 최신 버전은 26.12이고 그사이 메이저 버전이 열네 번 나왔습니다(참고: Node.js 26.12.0 릴리스 ). 숫자보다 큰 변화는 런타임의 역할입니다. 2019년의 Node.js는 서버와 빌드 도구를 실행하는 런타임이었다면, 지금의 Node.js는 TypeScript 파일을 바로 실행하고 테스트 러너와 SQLite, WebSocket 클라이언트를 내장하며 권한 모델로 파일과 네트워크 접근을 제한합니다. 2019년에 별도 패키지를 설치해야 했던 기능 상당수가 런타임에 내장되었습니다. 경쟁 구도도 달라졌습니다. 2019년에는 Node.js와 Deno를 비교했지만 지금은 Bun까지 세 런타임이 Node.js 호환성을 두고 경쟁합니다. 다만 2026년 10월 Deno 팀이 Cloudflare에 합류하면서 Deno 런타임의 개발은 1년 뒤 끝나게 되었습니다. 패키지 생태계에서는 2020년 GitHub이 npm을 인수하면서 2019년 글이 걱정한 "기술 외적인 불확실성"이 해소되었습니다. 그 대신 2025년부터는 공급망 공격이 가장 큰 문제가 되었습니다. 메인테이너 계정을 탈취해 악성 버전을 올리는 공격이 반복되었고 스스로 퍼지는 웜까지 등장했습니다. npm과 pnpm은 설치 스크립트를 기본으로 실행하지 않도록 바꾸었습니다. 표 1 2019년 이후 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 주요 사건 시기 사건 2020년 3월 GitHub, npm 인수 발표 (4월 인수 완료) 2021년 9월 Electron, 8주 릴리스 주기로 전환 (Electron 15) 2024년 10월 Deno 2 출시 , Tauri 2.0 출시 , React Native 0.76에서 새 아키텍처 기본화 2024년 12월 Node.js 22.12에서 require(esm) 플래그 제거 2025년 1월 WinterCG가 Ecma TC55(WinterTC)로 이동, pnpm 10에서 의존성 설치 스크립트 기본 미실행 2025년 9월 chalk, debug 등 메인테이너 계정 탈취 , Shai-Hulud 웜 2025년 11월 npm classic 토큰 생성 중단 , Shai-Hulud 2.0 2025년 12월 npm classic 토큰 전체 폐기 , Anthropic의 Bun 인수 , ECMA-429 1판 승인 2026년 3월 Node.js 릴리스 일정 개편 발표 , Axios 계정 탈취 2026년 7월 npm 12, 설치 스크립트 기본 미실행 2026년 8월 Bun 1.4 (Rust 재작성), pnpm 12 (Rust 재작성), vlt 1.0 2026년 10월 Deno 팀, Cloudflare 합류 , Deno 런타임 개발 사실상 종료(1년간 보안 업데이트 후 종료), Deno Deploy 6개월 뒤 종료 Node.js 2019년 글은 마무리에서 "Node.js는 주요 개발 선택 사항 중 하나로 당당하게 인정받고 있다"고 평가했습니다. 7년 뒤의 지표를 보면 이 평가는 더 굳어졌습니다. 그사이 Node.js는 ESM과 TypeScript 지원에서 큰 진전을 이뤘고 릴리스 방식도 바꾸었습니다. 지표로 보는 Node.js Stack Overflow 2025 개발자 설문에서 Node.js는 '웹 프레임워크와 기술' 항목 1위를 차지했습니다. 전체 응답자의 48.7%, 전문 개발자의 49.1%가 Node.js를 사용한다고 답했습니다. 같은 항목에서 Deno는 4%였고, Bun은 '클라우드 개발' 항목에서 5.5%였습니다(참고: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025: Technology ). State of JS 2025의 JavaScript 런타임 문항(응답자 11,141명)에서도 순서는 같습니다(표 2). 조사 측은 "Bun의 3위는 프로젝트 성장의 좋은 신호"라고 평했습니다(참고: State of JS 2025: Other Tools ). 표 2 State of JS 2025 JavaScript 런타임 사용 응답 수(출처: State of JS 2025 ) 런타임 응답 수 Node.js 10,062 브라우저 9,682 Bun 2,321 Service Workers 1,660 Cloudflare Workers 1,294 Deno 1,244 이 설문에서 Node.js의 사용 응답 수는 Bun과 Deno 각각의 네 배 이상입니다. 다만 Bun과 Deno가 Node.js 호환을 목표로 삼으면서 Node.js 코드를 실행할 수 있는 런타임이 Node.js만은 아니게 되었습니다. 릴리스 관리와 새 연간 일정 2019년 글에서 설명한 연 2회 메이저 릴리스 (짝수 버전은 장기 지원(LTS), 홀수 버전은 단기 지원)는 2026년까지 유지되었습니다. Node.js는 2026년 3월 릴리스 일정 개편을 발표했습니다(참고: Evolving the Node.js Release Schedule ). 약 10년간 이어 온 연 2회 메이저 릴리스를 Node.js 27부터 연 1회로 바꿉니다. 매년 4월 메이저 버전을 출시하고 10월에 LTS로 전환합니다. 홀짝 구분 없이 모든 버전이 LTS가 됩니다. 메이저 출시 전 6개월 동안 하위 호환을 깨는 변경(semver-major)을 허용하는 알파 채널( 27.0.0-alpha.1 형식)을 운영합니다. 버전 번호를 출시 연도에 맞춥니다. 27.0.0은 2027년, 28.0.0은 2028년에 나옵니다. 그림 1 Node.js 24부터 30까지의 릴리스 일정(27부터 새 일정 적용, 출처: Evolving the Node.js Release Schedule ) 발표문은 개편 이유로 홀수 버전의 채택률이 매우 낮았다는 데이터와, 대부분 자원봉사자인 메인테이너가 네다섯 개의 릴리스 라인에 보안 패치를 동시에 내보내는 부담을 들었습니다. 표 3 Node.js 릴리스 현황(2026년 10월, 출처: nodejs/Release ) 버전 상태 주요 내용 22(Jod) Maintenance LTS, 2027년 4월 종료 require(esm) 플래그 제거 24(Krypton) Active LTS, 10월 20일 Maintenance 전환 V8 13.6, using , Error.isError , RegExp.es

title: 2026년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - JavaScript(ECMAScript)
abstract: 2016년부터 매년 이어 오던 "JavaScript의 동향" 연재는 2020년을 마지막으로 한동안 쉬었습니다. 그사이 6년이 지났고, 그 6년 동안 ECMAScript 명세는 여섯 번 개정되었습니다. 2020년 글을 쓸 때 Stage 2였던 Temporal은 9년에 걸친 논의 끝에 Stage 4에 올랐고, 이제 Chrome과 Firefox, Node.js에서 플래그 없이 쓸 수 있습니다. 달라진 것은 명세만이 아닙니다. 2020년에는 상상하기 어려웠던 방식으로 코드를 쓰는 사람이 늘었습니다. AI 코딩 도구가 코드의 상당 부분을 작성하고, 사람이 방향을 정하면 AI 에이전트가 브라우저 엔진의 JavaScript 엔진 코드를 다른 언어로 옮기는 일까지 생겼습니다. 2025년 GitHub Octoverse에서 TypeScript가 처음으로 가장 많이 쓰인 언어 1위에 올랐고, GitHub은 그 배경으로 AI를 꼽았습니다. 이번 연재는 다음 네 편으로 구성됩니다. 1편: JavaScript(ECMAScript) 2편: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 3편: WebAssembly 4편: 라이브러리와 프레임워크 직전 회차인 2020년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - JavaScript(ECMAScript) 에서는 ECMAScript 2020, 2021과 당시 진행 중이던 제안들을 살펴보았습니다. 해마다 발표되는 명세는 'ECMAScript 2026'처럼 연도를 붙여 부르고, 줄여서 'ES2026'이라고도 씁니다. 이 글에서는 먼저 2020년 이후 6년의 공백을 정리하고, 2020년 글에서 소개한 제안들이 어떤 결말을 맞았는지 확인합니다. 이어서 TC39 프로세스의 변화, 2026년 6월 승인된 ECMAScript 2026과 2027년 명세에 포함될 기능, 브라우저와 임베디드 엔진의 현황, JavaScript 상표권 분쟁, TypeScript 7을 살펴봅니다. 마지막으로 AI 코딩 도구가 JavaScript와 TypeScript를 쓰는 방식, 그리고 표준을 만드는 방식에 어떤 영향을 주고 있는지 정리합니다. 이 글의 내용은 2026년 10월을 기준으로 작성되었습니다. 글을 읽는 시점에 따라 글의 내용과 사실이 다를 수 있습니다. 2020년 이후 6년 2020년 글은 swyx의 The Third Age of JavaScript 를 인용하며 2020년 이후를 JavaScript의 세 번째 주기로 보았습니다. 이 주기에서는 레거시를 정리하고 도구가 만든 레이어를 걷어 내는 일이 일어날 것이라고 했습니다. 구체적으로는 세 가지를 예상했습니다. CommonJS, AMD 같은 비표준 모듈이 ESM으로 전환될 것입니다. JavaScript 도구가 반드시 JavaScript로 작성될 필요는 없다는 흐름이 강해질 것입니다. TypeScript와 JavaScript가 서로 영향을 주며 함께 발전할 것입니다. 6년이 지난 지금 세 가지 모두 예상한 방향으로 진행되었습니다. 다만 속도와 모습은 예상과 달랐습니다. ESM 전환은 생각보다 오래 걸렸습니다. 전환을 가로막던 가장 큰 장벽은 CommonJS 코드에서 ESM 패키지를 require() 로 불러올 수 없다는 점이었고, 이 문제는 2024년 말이 되어서야 Node.js의 require(esm) 지원으로 풀렸습니다(참고: Node.js 22.12.0 (LTS) ). 인기 npm 패키지의 모듈 형식을 정기적으로 집계하는 wooorm/npm-esm-vs-cjs 데이터에 따르면, ESM을 제공하는(ESM 전용이거나 ESM과 CommonJS를 함께 제공하는) 패키지 비율은 2021년 8월 7.8%에서 2024년 11월 25.9%, 2026년 6월 38.0%로 늘었습니다. 다만 2025년 12월부터 집계 대상 목록의 출처가 바뀌어 그 이전 수치와 바로 비교하기는 어렵습니다. Anthony Fu (Vue, Vite, Nuxt 코어 팀원이자 Vitest, Slidev, UnoCSS 제작자)는 2024년 말 수치를 근거로 새 패키지는 ESM 전용으로 내자고 제안하기도 했습니다(참고: Move on to ESM-only ). 늘어난 것은 분명하지만 여전히 인기 패키지의 60% 이상은 ESM을 제공하지 않습니다. 그림 1 2021~2026년 인기 npm 패키지의 모듈 형식 비율 변화(esm과 dual의 합이 ESM 제공 비율, 출처: wooorm/npm-esm-vs-cjs ) 도구의 언어 전환은 예상보다 빨랐습니다. 2020년 글에서 Babel과 비교했던 SWC 외에도 esbuild(Go), Rolldown과 Oxc(Rust), Biome(Rust) 같은 도구가 주류가 되었습니다. 2025년 3월에는 TypeScript 컴파일러 자체를 Go로 옮기겠다는 발표가 나왔고, 2026년 7월 Go 기반의 TypeScript 7.0이 정식 출시되었습니다(참고: A 10x Faster TypeScript , Announcing TypeScript 7.0 ). 이 글에서는 언어와 런타임에 관련된 부분만 짧게 살펴봅니다. TypeScript는 '보편화'를 넘어 사실상 기본값이 되었습니다. Next.js, Astro, SvelteKit 같은 프레임워크가 프로젝트를 TypeScript로 생성하고, Node.js와 Deno, Bun 모두 .ts 파일을 별도 변환 없이 실행합니다. 예상하지 못한 변화도 있었습니다. 2020년 글은 AI에 대해 한 줄도 쓰지 않았습니다. 그러나 2026년 현재 JavaScript 생태계의 변화를 설명할 때 AI 코딩 도구를 빼놓기 어렵습니다. 이 내용은 "AI 도구로 인한 변화" 절에서 따로 정리합니다. 2020년 글에서 소개한 제안들의 결말 2020년 글의 "새로운 또는 완료되지 않은 제안들" 절에서 다룬 제안들은 다음과 같은 결말을 맞았습니다. 표 1 2020년 글에서 소개한 제안들의 현재 상태 제안 2020년 7월 2026년 10월 비고 Top-level await Stage 3 ES2022 2021년 5월 Stage 4 Class fields, private methods, static class features Stage 3 ES2022 2021년 Stage 4 KV Storage 모듈 중단 비활성 브라우저 벤더의 투자 없음 Pipeline Operator Stage 1 Stage 2 2021년 8월 Hack 스타일로 Stage 2 Records & Tuples Stage 1 철회 2025년 4월 철회, Composites로 이어짐 Temporal Stage 2 Stage 4 2026년 3월 Stage 4, ES2027 포함 예정 2020년 글에서 Stage 3에 머물러 있다고 했던 클래스 필드 관련 제안 세 개는 2021년 Stage 4에 올라 ES2022에 포함되었습니다(참고: 2021년 4월 회의록 ). Top-level await도 같은 명세에 포함되었습니다(참고: 2021년 5월 회의록 ). KV Storage는 2020년 이후 다시 논의되지 않았습니다. WICG 저장소에는 "브라우저 벤더 중 누구도 투자하지 않아 비활성 상태"라는 안내만 남아 있습니다(참고: KV Storage ). Pipeline Operator 는 2021년 8월 Hack 스타일 문법으로 Stage 2에 올랐습니다(참고: 2021년 8월 회의록 ). 2020년 글의 예시 코드처럼 함수 이름만 나열하는 F# 스타일 대신, 이전 단계의 값을 가리키는 토픽 토큰을 쓰는 방식입니다. 토큰으로 무엇을 쓸지는 아직 정해지지 않았고, 제안 문서는 임시로 % 를 씁니다. // 2020년 글의 예시 코드를 Hack 스타일로 다시 쓰면 let result = "hello" | > doubleSay ( % ) | > capitalize ( % ) | > exclaim ( % ) ; 이후로는 진척이 거의 없습니다. 2026년 9월 TC39 회의 안건에는 Stage 2.7 리뷰어가 정해지지 않은 Stage 2 제안 목록에 pipeline-operator가 올라 있었습니다(참고: TC39 116차 회의 안건 ). 이 회의 뒤인 10월에야 Ross Kirsling과 Christian Ulbrich가 리뷰어로 지정되었습니다(참고: tc39/

title: 글로벌 최고 수준의 자체 비전 인코더, Kanana-2-vision-encoder 개발기

title: 평균 CPU는 여유로운데, 커밋은 왜 느릴까?
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스증권 DBA Team 조규범입니다. 주문과 체결을 처리하는 API 뒤에는 Oracle DB가 있습니다. 이 DB에서 커밋이 늦어지면 커밋을 기다리던 세션이 모두 함께 멈추고, API 응답도 그만큼 늦어지는데요. 거래가 몰리는 정규장 시간에는 짧은 지연도 그냥 넘기기 어렵습니다. 그런데 어느 날부터 커밋 대기가 0.1초 넘게 이어지는 현상이 반복해서 보이기 시작했습니다. 스토리지, OS, 네트워크, 애플리케이션, Oracle을 차례로 확인했지만 평균 지표는 모두 정상 범위였어요. 호스트 CPU에도 여유가 있었고요. 원인은 CPU 소켓 하나에 몰려 있던 NIC 인터럽트였습니다. 인터럽트를 두 소켓으로 나누자 0.1초 이상의 커밋 대기는 대부분 개선됐고, 같은 조치를 적용한 다른 Oracle RAC에서는 동시접속자가 28% 많은 날에도 개장 직후 10분간 CPU 사용률이 36.6%에서 17.4%로 내려왔습니다. 이번 글에서는 평균 지표 뒤에 가려져 있던 병목을 어떻게 찾았는지, 그리고 왜 설정이 아니라 하드웨어 배치를 바꿔야 했는지 공유하려고 합니다. 그림 1. 개선 전후의 핵심 지표 평균 지표로는 보이지 않던 지연 커밋은 무엇을 기다릴까 Oracle에서 트랜잭션을 커밋하면, 변경 내용을 담은 리두 로그가 디스크에 기록된 뒤에야 커밋이 완료됩니다. 리두 로그 기록은 LGWR(log writer)라는 백그라운드 프로세스가 전담하는데요. 세션은 LGWR가 기록을 마칠 때까지 기다리고, 이 시간은 log file sync 라는 대기 이벤트로 확인할 수 있습니다. 인스턴스의 커밋 기록은 모두 LGWR를 거칩니다. 그래서 LGWR가 잠깐만 밀려도 그사이 커밋한 세션이 모두 함께 기다리게 되죠. 저희가 본 현상도 이것이었습니다. log file sync 대기가 0.1초 이상 이어지는 일이 반복됐어요. 지연은 특정 CPU에서만 생겼습니다 다섯 개 레이어를 모두 점검했지만 특이 사항은 없었습니다. 평균으로 보면 전부 정상 범위였기 때문입니다. 지연이 간헐적으로 생기다 보니 평균에 묻혔을 수 있다고 보고, LGWR 프로세스를 더 잘게 들여다보기로 했습니다. pidstat 으로 LGWR가 어느 CPU에서 실행되는지 기록해 보니 규칙이 보였습니다. 지연은 아무 때나 생기지 않았고, LGWR가 28번 CPU에서 실행될 때만 생기고 있었습니다. 그림 2. pidstat으로 LGWR의 실행 CPU를 추적한 결과. 관찰 당시를 재구성한 예시로, CPU 열과 지연이 생긴 시각이 겹치는 부분을 보면 됩니다. 같은 프로세스가 같은 일을 하는데 실행되는 CPU에 따라 결과가 다르다면, 원인은 Oracle보다 아래쪽인 OS나 하드웨어에 있을 가능성이 큽니다. 28번 CPU에서 LGWR 말고 다른 무언가가 함께 처리되고 있다는 뜻이니까요. 소켓 하나에 몰린 NIC 인터럽트 CPU별 인터럽트 확인하기 먼저 서버 구성을 짚고 가겠습니다. 이 서버에는 CPU 소켓 4개에 소켓당 물리 코어가 8개씩, 모두 32개의 물리 코어가 있습니다. 하이퍼스레딩을 켜 두어 OS에서는 논리 CPU 64개로 보이는데요. 아래에서 볼 /proc/interrupts 의 CPU 0–31은 물리 코어 스레드, 32–63은 하이퍼스레딩으로 생긴 논리 스레드입니다. /proc/interrupts 는 CPU별로 처리한 인터럽트 수를 장치마다 누적해서 보여 줍니다. 30초 간격으로 두 번 읽어 차이를 구하면, 그사이 각 CPU가 어떤 장치의 인터럽트를 얼마나 처리했는지 알 수 있습니다. 별도 도구 없이 cat 두 번이면 되는 방법이에요. 그림 3. /proc/interrupts 스냅샷 차분 예시. 행은 인터럽트 소스(NIC 큐), 열은 CPU입니다. 실제 수집값을 바탕으로 재구성했습니다. 숫자가 특정 열에만 쌓여 있다면, 그 큐의 인터럽트를 해당 CPU 하나가 전담하고 있다는 뜻입니다. 확인해 보니 NIC 인터럽트가 물리 코어 32개 중 8개에만 몰려 있었습니다. 논리 CPU로 세면 64개 중 16개입니다. 그런데 물리 코어 8개는 정확히 소켓 하나 분량이었어요. NIC 처리가 사실상 소켓 하나에서만 이뤄지고 있었던 거죠. 그림 4. 개선 전 CPU별 인터럽트 처리량 가장 바쁜 두 작업이 같은 코어에서 인터럽트를 처리하는 코어는 저마다 특정 NIC 포트의 큐를 하나씩 맡고 있었습니다. 그중 트래픽이 가장 많은 Oracle RAC 인터커넥트 포트의 인터럽트는 몇몇 코어에 더 집중돼 있었고요. 이슈 당시 따로 추적했을 때 LGWR 지연이 생기던 28번 CPU도 이렇게 인터럽트를 전담하던 코어 중 하나였습니다. RAC 인터커넥트는 두 노드가 캐시 블록을 주고받는 경로라, 클러스터에서 가장 바쁜 네트워크 경로입니다. LGWR 역시 DB에서 가장 바쁜 프로세스 중 하나고요. 이 두 작업이 같은 코어를 두고 경합하고 있었습니다. 왜 하필 소켓 하나였을까 하드웨어가 정해 둔 자리 이 서버는 소켓 4개가 각각 하나의 NUMA 노드를 이룹니다. 그리고 각 NIC 포트는 물리적으로 특정 소켓 하나에 연결되도록 설계돼 있는데요. NIC를 어느 슬롯에 꽂느냐에 따라, 그 포트의 인터럽트를 처리할 소켓이 정해지는 셈입니다. 여기에 인터커넥트 NIC 2장은 Active-Standby 본딩으로 묶여 있었습니다. 이중화를 위해 두 장을 묶었지만, 평소에는 활성 포트 하나로만 트래픽이 흐르는 방식입니다. 결국 인터커넥트 트래픽과 그 인터럽트가 모두 활성 포트가 연결된 소켓 하나로 몰렸습니다. NUMA 노드 : CPU 소켓 하나와 그 소켓에 직접 연결된 메모리의 묶음입니다. 이 서버는 4소켓이라 NUMA 노드도 4개입니다. IRQ(인터럽트) : 장치가 CPU에 처리를 요청하는 신호입니다. NIC는 패킷이 도착했음을 알릴 때 발생시키며(여러 건을 묶어 처리하기도 합니다), 일반 프로세스보다 먼저 처리됩니다. 본딩(Active-Standby / Active-Active) : NIC 2개를 하나처럼 묶는 이중화 방식입니다. Active-Standby는 하나만 쓰고 나머지는 대기시키고, Active-Active는 두 개를 동시에 씁니다. 인터럽트가 커밋을 늦추는 과정 NIC 인터럽트는 일반 프로세스보다 먼저 처리됩니다. LGWR가 하필 이 소켓의 코어에서 실행되고 있을 때 패킷이 도착하면, 다음과 같은 일이 벌어집니다. 상대 노드에서 패킷이 도착합니다. NIC가 인터럽트를 발생시킵니다. 커널이 실행 중이던 LGWR를 멈추고, 같은 코어에서 인터럽트를 먼저 처리합니다. 그만큼 리두 로그 기록이 밀립니다. 커밋을 기다리던 세션이 모두 함께 기다립니다. 한 번 밀리는 시간은 아주 짧습니다. 하지만 트래픽이 몰리는 구간에는 이 일이 계속 반복되면서 커밋 대기가 눈에 띄게 길어질 수 있습니다. 호스트 전체의 CPU에 여유가 있어도, 코어 하나가 바쁘면 그 코어에서 실행되는 프로세스는 기다려야 하는 거죠. 그림 5. NIC 인터럽트가 LGWR의 리두 로그 기록을 밀어내는 과정 인터럽트를 두 소켓으로 나누기 해결 방법으로 세 가지를 검토했습니다. 먼저 irqbalance로 인터럽트를 다시 분배해 보려 했습니다. 하지만 이 장비에서는 NIC 큐와 CPU의 매핑 제약 때문에 설정이 적용되지 않았고, 인터럽트는 여전히 같은 코어에 몰려 있었습니다. 다음으로는 taskset으로 LGWR를 다른 소켓의 CPU에 고정하는 방법을 생각했습니다. 인터럽트를 피해 LGWR를 옮기는 방식인데요. Oracle을 기동할 때마다 수동으로 설정해야 해서, 운영하다 보면 놓치기 쉽다고 판단했습니다. 마지막은 하드웨어 배치를 바꾸는 방법이었습니다. 인터커넥트 NIC 2장을 서로 다른 소켓에 연결된 슬롯으로 옮기고, 본딩을 Active-Active로 바꿔 두 포트를 동시에 쓰는 겁니다. 이렇게 하면 인터럽트가 자연스럽게 두 소켓으로 나뉘고, 기동할 때마다 챙길 설정도 남지 않습니다. 저희는 이 방법을 선택했습니다. 그림 6. 본딩 전환 전후의 NIC와 소켓 연결 무엇이 달라졌을까 인터럽트는 실제로 나뉘었을까 같은 피크 시간대에 다시 스냅샷을 떠 보니, 초당 1,000건 넘게 인터럽트를 처리하는 물리 코어가 8개에서 15개로 늘었습니다. 논리 CPU로는 16개에서 31

title: 모델만 바꿨는데 LLM 비용이 3배가 된 이유
abstract: 안녕하세요, 당근 커뮤니티홈팀에서 백엔드를 개발하는 제이(Jay)예요. 당근 앱의 커뮤니티 탭에는 이웃이 알려 주는 동네 정보부터 소소한 일상과 취미까지 나누는 동네생활, 모임, 카페, 아파트가 모여 있어요. 커뮤니티홈팀은 이 서비스들의 글을 한데 모아 보여 주는 피드를 맡고 있어요. 피드를 맡으며 가장 고민하는 건 사용자에게 더 알맞은 글을 어떻게 보여 줄지예요. 그래서 기존 머신러닝 추천에 더해, LLM으로 글의 다양한 메타데이터를 뽑아 추천에 쓰고 있어요. 그중 하나가 LLM에 카테고리 목록과 글을 주고 어느 주제에 속하는지 고르게 하는 주제 분류예요. 추천은 보여 줄 글 후보를 모으는 단계와 그 순서를 정하는 단계로 나뉘는데, 글마다 주제가 붙어 있으면 첫 단계부터 사용자가 관심 있는 주제의 글을 골라 올 수 있어요. 주제 분류를 할 때 LLM에 보내는 요청을 열어 보면 대부분이 매번 똑같은 지시문과 카테고리 목록이고, 글 본문은 끝에 조금 붙어 있을 뿐이에요. 이 글에서는 요청마다 똑같은 이 부분을 고정부라고 부를게요. 2026년 8월, 이 작업의 모델을 Gemini에서 단가가 20% 낮은 OpenAI GPT-5.6으로 바꿨어요. 응답은 정상이었고 에러도 한 건 없었어요. 닷새 뒤 보니 단가는 내렸는데 요청당 비용은 3.2배가 돼 있었어요. 원인은 프롬프트 캐시였어요. 입력 중 캐시에서 읽어 온 비율인 캐시 히트율이 85.8%에서 2.3%로 떨어져 있었죠. 교체 전후의 응답을 나란히 놓으면 달라진 곳은 사용량 정보 안의 캐시 필드 하나뿐이었어요. 캐시가 깨져도 에러는 나지 않아요. 비용만 늘어요. 이 글은 그 일을 해결하며 알게 된 것을 정리한 기록이에요. 캐시가 무엇을 재사용하는지, 비용은 어떻게 매겨지는지, 언제 켜지고 어디까지 저장되는지, 캐시에서 읽었는지는 어떻게 확인하는지를 OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini를 나란히 놓고 살펴봐요. 같은 지시문에 입력만 바꿔 LLM을 대량으로 부르거나, 챗봇이나 에이전트처럼 앞부분이 같은 요청을 되풀이해 보내는 분이라면 참고가 될 거예요. 프롬프트 캐시의 원리 신입 검수자에게 매번 규정집 20쪽과 오늘 볼 글 한 편을 함께 준다고 해 볼게요. 규정집은 늘 같고 글만 바뀌는데, 이 검수자는 기억을 못 해서 글마다 규정집을 처음부터 다시 읽어요. 하루 10만 편이면 규정집을 10만 번 읽는 셈이에요. LLM도 똑같이 요청마다 프롬프트 전체를 처음부터 다시 읽어요. 이 낭비를 줄이는 게 프롬프트 캐시예요. 앞 토큰을 돌아보는 어텐션 LLM은 글을 토큰 단위로 하나씩 이어 써요. 다음 토큰을 고르기 전에는 앞 토큰들을 돌아보며 무엇을 참고할지 따지는데, 이 계산을 어텐션(attention)이라고 해요. “어제 시장에서 산 사과를 깎아서” 다음에 올 토큰을 고른다고 해 볼게요. 사람은 바로 “먹었다”를 떠올려요. “사과”와 “깎아서”가 가장 관련 있고 “어제”나 “시장에서”는 덜 중요하다는 걸 알기 때문이에요. 모델은 이 판단을 마지막 토큰 “깎아서” 자리에서 숫자로 해요. 어텐션에는 토큰마다 세 가지 값이 쓰여요. 도서관에서 자료를 찾는 일에 비유해 볼게요. Q(Query, 질문) : 마지막 토큰이 다음 토큰을 고르려고 들고 있는 질문이에요. “무엇을 했는지 이어 쓰려면 어떤 정보가 필요하지?” 같은 것이에요. K(Key, 분류표) : 앞 토큰마다 붙은 꼬리표예요. 책의 분류표처럼 “먹을 수 있는 물건”, “때를 나타내는 말” 같은 정보를 담아요. V(Value, 내용) : 앞 토큰이 실제로 건네주는 정보예요. 책의 본문에 해당해요. 마지막 토큰 “깎아서”는 자기 Q를 앞 토큰들(자기 자신 포함)의 K와 하나씩 맞춰 보고 점수를 매겨요. “사과”와 “깎아서”는 높은 점수를, “어제”는 낮은 점수를 받아요. 그다음 점수 비율대로 V를 섞고 그 결과로 다음 토큰 “먹었다”를 골라요. 분류표(K)로 관련 있는 책을 고른 뒤, 그 책들의 본문(V)을 점수만큼 읽는 것과 같아요. 실제 Q, K, V는 사람이 읽을 수 있는 문장이 아니라 숫자 묶음(벡터)이고, 위 설명은 그 역할을 말로 푼 거예요. 한 번 만들면 계속 쓰는 K와 V “먹었다”를 고른 뒤에는 “먹었다”가 Q를 들고 같은 일을 해요. 이때 “어제”부터 “깎아서”까지의 K와 V는 앞 단계에서 만든 것과 똑같아요. 뒤에 어떤 토큰이 붙어도 앞 토큰의 K와 V는 바뀌지 않거든요. 그래서 모델은 한 번 만든 K와 V를 캐시에 쌓아 두고 다시 꺼내 써요. 이 캐시를 KV 캐시라고 해요. 새로 계산하는 건 새 토큰의 Q, K, V뿐이고, Q는 그 토큰이 앞을 볼 때 한 번 쓰고 끝나서 쌓아 두지 않아요. 캐시가 없다면 토큰을 하나 쓸 때마다 앞 토큰 전부를 처음부터 다시 계산해야 해요. 입력도 마찬가지예요. 모델은 답을 쓰기 전에 입력 전체를 한꺼번에 읽으며 K와 V를 만들어 캐시를 채워요. 이 단계를 prefill이라고 하는데, 입력이 길수록 오래 걸려요. title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

title: What Makes a Good Symbol for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Planning?
abstract: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions. Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful. In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm--centric view to define usefulness: a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem. We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention. We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes. Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.

title: Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: A fine-tuned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy can easily place the alphabet soup in the basket on command, just as it saw during fine-tuning. However, if the basket is shifted five centimeters to the left, it drops the soup off the table. We developed an interpretability pipeline to investigate what such a policy is computing. Injecting task A's activations into the action expert while the policy looks at task B's scene makes pi0.5 execute task A's motor trajectory in 99.6\% of episodes (n{=}1{,}968). The injected program is bound to absolute workspace coordinates and ignores the visible scene, which provides a mechanistic account of the perturbation brittleness that concurrent benchmarks report. The binding holds on a physical UR10e: directed replay redirects the commanded task in 26/26 rollouts in one direction and 18/26 in the other, with no-injection and random-direction controls at the floor, and once the source object is moved 10--15\,cm the arm grasps and releases at the recorded coordinates in 50/50 trials, picking up the wrong block when one sits there and closing on empty air when none does. Applying the same interventions to six VLAs on LIBERO, MetaWorld, SimplerEnv, and ALOHA over 420{,}000+ rollouts yields three further findings: every architecture encodes the instruction, and four of the five weight it below vision whenever the scene alone identifies the goal; under the standard replacement write-back the SAE pooling that preserves behavior is architecture-specific (pi0.5 per-token, SmolVLA indifferent), and goal selection and motor generation separate into VLM and expert pathways wherever the two are distinguishable. We release Action Atlas (https://action-atlas.com), an interactive platform covering all 520+ trained SAEs, 79 identified concepts, and the scored UR10e rollouts. Code: https://github.com/CWRU-AISM/action-atlas

title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness.
